blocks.body:
The series $\sum_{n\ge1} n^{-s}$ converges only when $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$. Yet number theorists talk freely about $\zeta(\tfrac12 + 14.13i)$ and about $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12}$. What can those values mean, if the series that defines $\zeta$ diverges there?

The answer is analytic continuation. A holomorphic function on a connected region is so rigid that its values on any small disc determine it everywhere. So if a function given on a small region extends holomorphically to a larger one at all, it does so in exactly one way, and the extension deserves the same name. This lesson proves that uniqueness, shows how continuations are built in practice, and does it for the zeta function.

blocks.title: The identity theorem
blocks.body: Let $U$ be a connected open set and let $f, g$ be holomorphic on $U$. If $f = g$ on a set of points that has an accumulation point in $U$ (for example on a small disc, or on a short segment), then $f = g$ on all of $U$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $h = f - g$, and let $S$ be the set of points $z \in U$ at which $h$ and all its derivatives vanish.

$S$ is open: if $z_0 \in S$, the Taylor series of $h$ at $z_0$ is identically zero, and it converges to $h$ on a disc around $z_0$ ([[holomorphic]]), so $h \equiv 0$ on that disc, and so do all its derivatives.

$S$ is closed in $U$: it is the intersection of the sets $\{h^{(n)} = 0\}$, each closed because $h^{(n)}$ is continuous.

$S$ is non-empty: let $z_0 \in U$ be an accumulation point of zeros of $h$; then $h(z_0) = 0$ by continuity. If some derivative of $h$ were nonzero at $z_0$, let $m$ be the least such order. The power series then gives $h(z) = (z - z_0)^m k(z)$ with $k$ holomorphic near $z_0$ and $k(z_0) \ne 0$. By continuity $k \ne 0$ near $z_0$, so $h$ has no zeros in a small punctured disc around $z_0$, contradicting the choice of $z_0$. So $z_0 \in S$.

A connected set cannot be split into two disjoint non-empty open sets, so $S$, being open, closed and non-empty, is all of $U$. Hence $h \equiv 0$.

blocks.title: Analytic continuation
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be holomorphic on an open set $U$, and let $V \supseteq U$ be a connected open set. A holomorphic function $F$ on $V$ with $F = f$ on $U$ is an analytic continuation of $f$ to $V$. By the identity theorem there is at most one.

Continuation is a statement about functions, not about formulas. The formula that defines $f$ on $U$ (a series, an integral) may make no sense on $V$; the continuation is whatever holomorphic function on $V$ agrees with it.

blocks.title: The model example
blocks.body:
The geometric series $$\sum_{n\ge0} z^n = \frac{1}{1-z} \qquad (|z| < 1)$$ diverges for every $|z| \ge 1$, since then its terms do not tend to $0$. But the right side is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\}$, which is connected, so $1/(1-z)$ is the analytic continuation of the series to $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\}$. Its value at $z = 2$ is $-1$. Nobody claims that $1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + \cdots$ converges to $-1$; the statement is that the function defined by the series near $0$ continues to a function whose value at $2$ is $-1$.

When no closed formula is available, continuation can be done step by step. Re-expand around a new centre $a$ with $|a| < 1$: $$\frac{1}{1-z} = \frac{1}{(1-a) - (z-a)} = \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(z-a)^n}{(1-a)^{n+1}},$$ which converges for $|z - a| < |1 - a|$. For $a = -\tfrac12$ the new disc has radius $\tfrac32$ and pokes out of the unit disc on the left; it reaches $z = -1.2$, for example. Moving the centre again and again (Weierstrass's chain of discs) reaches every point except $1$. This procedure works for any power series, and it is how one decides in principle whether a continuation exists.

blocks.title: Obstructions: natural boundaries and many-valuedness
blocks.body:
Not every function continues. The series $f(z) = \sum_{n\ge0} z^{2^n}$ converges on $|z| < 1$, but it cannot be continued across any arc of the unit circle. Indeed, if $\zeta^{2^k} = 1$ then $\zeta^{2^n} = 1$ for all $n \ge k$, so for $0 < r < 1$ $$f(r\zeta) = \sum_{n< k}(r\zeta)^{2^n} + \sum_{n\ge k} r^{2^n},$$ and the second sum tends to $+\infty$ as $r \to 1$. Such points $\zeta$ are dense on the circle, so $f$ is unbounded near every arc, which a continuation across the arc would forbid. The unit circle is a natural boundary.

Continuation can also be ambiguous in a different way: continuing along two different paths around a point can give different answers. Continuing $\log z$ once around the origin returns $\log z + 2\pi i$. On a simply connected region this cannot happen (the monodromy theorem, whose proof we omit), so on such regions a function that can be continued along every path has a single-valued continuation.

blocks.title: Continuing the zeta function
blocks.body:
For $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$ let $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}$; it is holomorphic there (each partial sum is entire, and the convergence is uniform on each half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\, s \ge 1 + \delta$; uniform limits of holomorphic functions are holomorphic, see [[uniform-convergence]]). Here is a continuation to $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$.

For an integer $N \ge 1$, compute $s\int_1^N \lfloor t\rfloor t^{-s-1}\,dt$ by splitting at the integers: on $[n, n+1)$ the floor is $n$, and $s\int_n^{n+1} t^{-s-1}\,dt = n^{-s} - (n+1)^{-s}$. So $$s\int_1^N \lfloor t\rfloor t^{-s-1}\,dt = \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} n\bigl(n^{-s} - (n+1)^{-s}\bigr) = \sum_{n=1}^{N} n^{-s} - N^{1-s},$$ after rearranging the finite sum. Let $N \to \infty$ with $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$, so that $N^{1-s} \to 0$, and write $\lfloor t\rfloor = t - \{t\}$: $$\zeta(s) = s\int_1^\infty \lfloor t\rfloor t^{-s-1}\,dt = \frac{s}{s-1} - s\int_1^\infty \{t\}\,t^{-s-1}\,dt.$$ Now look at the right side. Since $0 \le \{t\} < 1$, the last integral converges absolutely whenever $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$, uniformly on each half-plane $\mathrm{Re}\, s \ge \delta > 0$, and it defines a holomorphic function there (each truncation $\int_1^N$ is entire in $s$). So the right side is holomorphic on $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$ except at $s = 1$, where $\frac{s}{s-1} = 1 + \frac{1}{s-1}$ has a simple pole with residue $1$. By the identity theorem this is the continuation of $\zeta$ to $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$. For example it gives $\zeta(\tfrac12) \approx -1.4604$, even though $\sum n^{-1/2}$ diverges.

To go further, Riemann (1859) proved the functional equation $$\zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi s}{2}\right)\Gamma(1-s)\,\zeta(1-s),$$ which expresses $\zeta$ on $\mathrm{Re}\, s < 0$ in terms of its values on $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 1$, where the series converges. Together these continue $\zeta$ to a function holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\}$. Its proof is in [[functional-equation]] and uses the [[gamma]] function.

blocks.title: Continuing the gamma function
blocks.body: The gamma function is defined for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$ by $\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$, and it is holomorphic there. Use $\Gamma(s+1) = s\Gamma(s)$ to continue it to $\mathbb{C}$ minus the non-positive integers, and find its residue at $s = -n$.
blocks.solution:
Integration by parts gives $\Gamma(s+1) = s\Gamma(s)$ for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$. Iterating, for each integer $n \ge 0$, $$\Gamma(s) = \frac{\Gamma(s + n + 1)}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)} \qquad (\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0).$$ The right side makes sense and is holomorphic for $\mathrm{Re}\, s > -n-1$, except at $s = 0, -1, \ldots, -n$. So it continues $\Gamma$ to that larger region. The continuations for different $n$ agree where both are defined (they agree on $\mathrm{Re}\, s > 0$, and the region where both are defined is connected), so together they give a single function holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0, -1, -2, \ldots\}$.

At $s = -n$ the factor $s + n$ in the denominator vanishes and the numerator equals $\Gamma(1) = 1$. So the pole is simple, and $$\mathrm{Res}(\Gamma, -n) = \lim_{s\to -n}(s+n)\Gamma(s) = \frac{1}{(-n)(-n+1)\cdots(-1)} = \frac{(-1)^n}{n!}.$$

blocks.title: Values at negative integers
blocks.body: Use the functional equation to compute $\zeta(-1)$, and explain the zeros of $\zeta$ at $s = -2, -4, -6, \ldots$.
blocks.solution:
Put $s = -1$: $\zeta(-1) = 2^{-1}\pi^{-2}\sin(-\pi/2)\,\Gamma(2)\,\zeta(2) = \frac12\cdot\frac{1}{\pi^2}\cdot(-1)\cdot 1\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{6} = -\frac{1}{12}$.

At $s = -2k$ with $k \ge 1$, the factor $\sin(\pi s/2) = \sin(-\pi k) = 0$, while $\Gamma(1 + 2k) = (2k)!$ and $\zeta(1 + 2k)$ are finite and nonzero. So $\zeta(-2k) = 0$: these are the trivial zeros. In general $\zeta(-n) = -B_{n+1}/(n+1)$ for $n \ge 1$, with $B_j$ the Bernoulli numbers; for instance $\zeta(-3) = \tfrac{1}{120}$. Also $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ (here the functional equation must be read as a limit, since $\sin(0) = 0$ meets the pole of $\zeta(1-s)$).

The often-quoted "$1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots = -\tfrac1{12}$" is shorthand for $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12}$, a value of the continued function. The series itself diverges.

blocks.title: Prescribed values on a sequence
blocks.body:
(a) Is there a function $f$, holomorphic on the open unit disc, with $f(1/n) = (-1)^n/n$ for every integer $n \ge 2$?

(b) Is there one with $f(1/n) = 1/(n+1)$ for every $n \ge 2$? If so, is it unique?
blocks.solution:
(a) No. Suppose $f$ exists. On the points $1/(2k)$ we have $f(1/(2k)) = 1/(2k)$, so $f$ agrees with $g(z) = z$ on a set accumulating at $0$, which is inside the disc. By the identity theorem $f(z) = z$ everywhere. But then $f(1/3) = 1/3$, whereas it should be $-1/3$.

(b) Yes: $f(z) = \dfrac{z}{1+z}$ is holomorphic on the unit disc (its only pole is at $-1$, on the boundary) and $f(1/n) = \dfrac{1/n}{1 + 1/n} = \dfrac{1}{n+1}$. It is unique, because two such functions agree on $\{1/n\}$, which accumulates at $0$.

blocks.body:
- Continuation does not sum a divergent series. It produces a function; a "value" of a divergent series is only meaningful relative to the family of functions you embed it in. For example $1 + 1 + 1 + \cdots$ is $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$ if you view it as $\sum n^{-s}$ at $s = 0$, but it sits at the pole of $\sum z^n$ if you view it as that series at $z = 1$.
- The accumulation point must lie inside the domain. $\sin(\pi/z)$ vanishes at every $z = 1/n$, but it is not identically zero on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$: the zeros accumulate only at $0$, which is not in the domain.
- Connectedness is essential. On the union of two disjoint discs, the function equal to $0$ on one and $1$ on the other is holomorphic.
- Nothing like this holds for real smooth functions. The function equal to $e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x \ne 0$ and $0$ at $0$ is infinitely differentiable, has all derivatives zero at $0$, and is not identically zero.
- A continuation along a path can depend on the path when the region has holes, as $\log z$ shows; uniqueness is only guaranteed on a fixed connected domain.

Riemann's 1859 paper continued $\zeta$ to the whole plane, proved the [[functional-equation]], linked the zeros of $\zeta$ to the distribution of primes and stated the Riemann hypothesis ([[rh]]). Continuation is the first step in the theory of the [[zeta]] function, of the [[gamma]] function, and of every [[dirichlet-series]] that matters in number theory: Dirichlet [[l-functions]], [[dedekind-zeta]] functions and [[hecke-l]] functions all have continuations and functional equations, and the hypotheses about their zeros are about the continued functions, in regions where the original series diverge. The zeros of the continued zeta function are the subject of [[nontrivial-zeros]].
